name: Button
description: A widget that enables users to trigger an action or event, such as submitting a form, opening a dialog, canceling an action, or performing a delete operation.

roles.description: Identifies the element as a button (not needed on native <button>)

required_attributes.description: Computed from text content, aria-labelledby, or aria-label

optional_attributes.description: Toggle-button state. Do NOT combine with role='switch' or aria-expanded — one state mechanism per control.
Only when the button shows/hides content — that makes it a disclosure. See patterns/disclosure.md.
Indicates the button opens a menu popup
Keeps the button focusable while marking it unavailable — unlike `disabled`, which removes it from the tab order entirely. Prefer this when the user needs to discover WHY it is unavailable.

notes: Always <button type="button">. Omitting type inside a <form> defaults to type="submit" — an enormous source of accidental submissions.
A control that NAVIGATES is a link (<a href>), not a button. A control that ACTS is a button. Enter activates both; Space only activates buttons; only links offer 'open in new tab'.
An icon-only button needs an accessible name: aria-label, or visually hidden text. The <svg> inside must be aria-hidden='true' focusable='false'.

`disabled` removes the button from the tab order, so a keyboard user cannot reach it to find out why it is unavailable, and cannot receive a tooltip on it. aria-disabled='true' keeps it focusable and announced as dimmed.
Do not stack state attributes: aria-pressed AND aria-expanded on one button announces two states and means neither clearly.
Disabled buttons are exempt from contrast requirements, but that does not make an unreadable one acceptable.
native_element: <button type="button"> — there is essentially no valid reason to build this from a div

raweb_criteria.reason: Role, name and any state (aria-pressed/aria-expanded) must be exposed.
Must activate with both Enter and Space, and with any pointing device.
Only if it is really a link: a control that navigates must be an <a href>, and its name must describe the destination.
In a form, the button's label must say what it does — 'Submit' is weaker than 'Create account'.
